hindi: माना कि $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=x^{3}+2x-2$ द्वारा परिभाषित है, तथा $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f$ का प्रतिलोम फलन है। माना कि $P$ एक ऐसा बिन्दु है जिस पर वक्र $y=f(x)$ तथा $y=g(x)$ प्रतिच्छेद करते हैं, तथा $P$ पर इन दोनों वक्रों के बीच का न्यून कोण $\theta$ है। तब $\tan\theta$ बराबर है
solution: $f'(x)=3x^{2}+2>0$: $f$ strictly increasing, and onto $\mathbb{R}$ (cubic), so $g$ exists
Graphs of $f$ and $g$ are mirror images in $y=x$; for increasing $f$ they meet only on $y=x$ (if $f(a)=b,\ f(b)=a$ with $a<b$ then $b<a$)
solution_full: $f'(x)=3x^{2}+2>0$ for all $x$, so $f$ is strictly increasing and one-one; a cubic tends to $\pm\infty$ at $\pm\infty$ and is continuous, so $f$ is onto $\mathbb{R}$. Hence $g=f^{-1}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ exists.

The graph of $g$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the line $y=x$. Suppose $(a,b)$ lies on both curves: $b=f(a)$ and $b=g(a)$, i.e. $f(b)=a$. If $a<b$ then, $f$ being increasing, $f(a)<f(b)$, i.e. $b<a$, a contradiction; similarly $a>b$ is impossible. So $a=b$ and $P$ lies on $y=x$ with $f(a)=a$.
$f(x)=x$ gives $x^{3}+x-2=0$, i.e. $(x-1)(x^{2}+x+2)=0$; the quadratic has discriminant $1-8<0$, so $x=1$ and $P=(1,1)$ is the only common point.
Slope of $y=f(x)$ at $P$: $m_1=f'(1)=3+2=5$. By the derivative of the inverse, $g'(1)=\dfrac{1}{f'(g(1))}=\dfrac{1}{f'(1)}=\dfrac15=m_2$ (the reflected tangent has the reciprocal slope).
The acute angle between the tangents satisfies $\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\dfrac{5-\frac15}{1+1}=\dfrac{24/5}{2}=\dfrac{12}{5}$.
Option (A) omits the denominator $1+m_1m_2=2$, (C) is $\cot\theta$, and (D) is $\sin\theta=\dfrac{12}{13}$.
originality_note: New: the angle at which a curve meets the graph of its own inverse, built from the mirror symmetry (common point on y=x for an increasing function) and the reciprocal slope of the inverse (way 5). Closest known: g'(b)=1/f'(a) evaluation questions and the angle between two given curves. Different because: the second curve is never written down; its slope comes only from the inverse-derivative rule, and the intersection point must be argued to lie on y=x.

concept_use.Inverse of a function: existence, graph: f is strictly increasing and onto, so g exists; the graphs are mirror images in y=x and therefore meet only on y=x, at P(1,1).
concept_use.Derivative of inverse of a function: The slope of y=g(x) at P is g'(1)=1/f'(1)=1/5, used in the angle formula.

stem_review: Read as a student: f, g with domains defined; 'a point P' is fine because the common point is unique (checked: x^3+x-2 has one real root). tan theta = 12/5 verified symbolically and by a numerical derivative of the inverse (0.2). Changed: wrote 'a point at which' instead of 'the point' to avoid presupposing uniqueness.
key_step: Arguing that an increasing function meets its inverse only on y=x, then g'(1)=1/f'(1).
justification: Two ideas linked (symmetry of inverse graphs with the increasing-function argument, and the derivative of the inverse) plus the angle formula; options help checking. Comparable to 2025-P2-Q14 (L3, derivative of f o g^{-1}) and above 2026-P2-Q17 (L2, angle between tangents).
